class.name: Struct
class.brief_description: A value with a fixed set of named, typed fields.
class.description:
A struct is a value type whose fields are declared once by a [StructLayout]: each field has a name, a static type and a default value. Every struct value carries a reference to its layout, so two values are equal only if they share the same layout and all of their fields are equal. Layouts come from two places. The engine registers its own at startup, such as [code]PhysicsRayResult3D[/code] returned by [method PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D.intersect_ray_struct]. GDScript declares its own with the [code]struct[/code] keyword: [codeblock] struct Point: var x: float = 0.0 var y: float = 0.0
func _ready(): var p := Point(1.0, 2.0) p.y += 1.0 print(p) # Prints "Point(x: 1.0, y: 3.0)" [/codeblock] In GDScript a layout name is a type: [code]var p: Point[/code], [code]Array[Point][/code], parameters and return types all work, and field access on a typed struct is checked at compile time. Calling the layout name like a function constructs a value: positional arguments fill the leading fields and the rest keep their defaults. A script struct can declare methods. Inside a method, [code]self[/code] is the value the method was called on and its fields can be used by name. Follow the convention of the built-in value types: a method returns a new value rather than changing [code]self[/code], like [method Vector2.normalized], and callers assign the result ([code]p = p.scaled(2.0)[/code]). This works on any expression, including array elements. A method that does assign to a field modifies the variable it was called on, so [code]p.scale(2.0)[/code] changes [code]p[/code]; such a method can only be called on a variable, parameter, member or field, not on a temporary or an array element, and calling it on a parameter changes only the parameter's copy. Methods with reserved names overload operators: [code]_add[/code], [code]_sub[/code], [code]_mul[/code], [code]_div[/code], [code]_mod[/code] for [code]+ - * / %[/code] with the struct on the left, [code]_neg[/code] for unary minus, and [code]_lt[/code], [code]_le[/code], [code]_gt[/code], [code]_ge[/code] for comparisons (which [method Array.sort] also uses). Operator methods take one parameter, none for [code]_neg[/code], and must not modify [code]self[/code]. [codeblock] struct Vec: var x: float = 0.0 var y: float = 0.0
func length() -> float: return sqrt(x * x + y * y)
func scale(f: float) -> void: x *= f y *= f
func _add(other: Vec) -> Vec: return Vec(x + other.x, y + other.y) [/codeblock] Structs have value semantics. Assigning one to another variable or passing it to a function copies the value, and assigning to a field of a copy never changes the original. The copy is lazy, so passing a struct around is as cheap as passing an [Array]. A struct can be saved in a scene or resource file and sent over the network; the layout is looked up by name when it is loaded. [b]Note:[/b] Unlike a [Dictionary], a struct cannot gain or lose fields, and assigning a value of the wrong type to a field is an error.

constructor.name: Struct
constructor.description: Constructs an empty struct with no layout. It has no fields and compares equal only to another empty struct. Use a layout name in GDScript, or [method PhysicsDirectSpaceState3D.intersect_ray_struct] and similar engine methods, to obtain a struct with fields.

constructor.name: Struct
constructor.description: Returns the same struct as [param from]. Since structs are values, the copy is independent of the original.

operator.name: operator !=
operator.description: Returns [code]true[/code] if the structs have different layouts or any field differs. See [method @GlobalScope.is_same] for comparing by identity instead.

operator.name: operator ==
operator.description: Returns [code]true[/code] if both structs share the same layout and every field compares equal with [code]==[/code].
